title: Solar water pump to a raised tank
summary: Run a 12V DC pump (RV or boat diaphragm pump, bilge pump or small submersible) from a solar panel to fill a raised tank, then let gravity supply taps and irrigation. A 50–100W panel can lift about 1,000 L a day through 5–10 m. A float switch stops it when the tank is full.

materials.item: 12V DC water pump: diaphragm (RV, boat, sprayer) or submersible/bilge
Float switch at the top of the tank
Relay, if the float switch is rated below the pump current
Tank or drums, 200–1,000 L, food-grade if the water is for drinking
Hose or pipe 12–25 mm for suction and delivery, food-safe if the water is for drinking
Strainer or screen for the intake
Check (non-return) valve to hold the prime
Fuse and holder, about 1.5× pump current
Battery and charge controller, to pump on demand or in cloud
Charge controller, if using a battery
Tank stand: timber, blocks or steel, rated for the full tank

steps.text: Measure the job: litres per day, and total lift from the water's surface to the top of the tank. Work out the power you need with the notes.
Test the pump on a 12V battery through a fuse: measure its current and time how fast it fills a bucket at no lift. Diaphragm pumps self-prime; bilge and centrifugal pumps must sit under water.
Place the pump as low and close to the water as you can. A diaphragm pump can suck up only 1–3 m in practice; pushing water up is easy, pulling it up is hard.
Fit a strainer on the intake and a check valve on the suction line so the pump stays primed overnight.
Build the tank stand on firm, level ground. Water weighs 1 kg per litre: a 1,000 L tank weighs a tonne.
steps.warn: A tank stand that tips or collapses can kill. Brace it in both directions and build for at least the full weight plus a margin.

steps.text: Run the delivery pipe to the top of the tank. Fit an overflow pipe that leads back to the source or away from the stand's footing.
Mount the float switch so it opens the circuit when the tank is nearly full. If its contacts are rated below the pump's current, let it switch a relay that switches the pump.

Wire: panel + → fuse → float switch (or relay) → pump +; pump − → panel −. With a battery, wire panel → controller → battery, and take the pump from the controller's load output or the battery through its own fuse.
steps.warn: Fuse every circuit at the battery. Check polarity before connecting: some pumps are damaged by reverse polarity.

steps.text: Mount the panel facing the equator, tilted at about your latitude, clear of shade.
steps.warn: Use a ladder with a second person on roofs and stands.

steps.text: Commission: watch the first fill. Check for leaks, measure flow in full sun, and check the float switch stops the pump.
Keep the strainer clear. Don't let a centrifugal pump run dry. Drain pump and pipes before frost. Treat the stored water before drinking: pumping doesn't purify it.

notes:
## Power maths
Lifting energy (Wh) = litres × total lift (m) ÷ 367. Small DC pumps are 20–40% efficient.
- 1,000 L up 8 m: 1,000 × 8 ÷ 367 ≈ 22Wh of lifting. At 25% pump efficiency, ≈ 87Wh from the panel.
- Panel watts ≈ daily Wh ÷ (sun hours × 0.6) for direct drive. 87 ÷ (3 × 0.6) ≈ 50W. Use 80–100W for cloudy days.

Total lift = height difference + pipe friction. Narrow hoses add a lot: keep delivery pipes 13 mm or bigger for 5–10 L/min.

## Pump types
| Pump | Typical | Lift | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| RV/boat diaphragm | 12V 3–7A, 10–20 L/min open | up to 20–40 m (2–4 bar) | Self-priming; pressure switch built in; tolerates brief dry running |
| Bilge pump | 12V 2–10A, 30–120 L/min open | 2–4 m before flow stops | Must be submerged; cheap; huge flow at low lift |
| Sprayer pump | 12V 2–5A | 10–30 m | Similar to RV pumps |
| Car windscreen washer pump | 12V 2–4A | a few metres | Short duty only; overheats if run long |

Don't use fuel pumps for water.

## Direct drive or battery
- **Direct drive (no battery):** simplest; pumps whenever the sun shines; flow follows sunlight. A tank is your battery.
- **Battery:** pump at any time, steady flow, more parts and losses.

## Suction limit
Atmospheric pressure can only push water up about 10 m into a perfect vacuum; real pumps manage 1–6 m, less at altitude. For deeper water, lower the pump or use a submersible.

## Gravity supply
Each metre of height gives about 0.1 bar. A tank 3 m up gives 0.3 bar: fine for a hose or drip irrigation, weak for a shower.

## Troubleshooting
- Pump runs but no water: lost prime, air leak on the suction side, or the lift is too high for it.
- Starts and stops in the morning: panel voltage near the pump's minimum. Normal in direct drive; a battery fixes it.
- Float switch works backwards: it's wired for emptying (sump use). Turn it over or use its other contact.

## If you lack a part
- No float switch: a reed switch and a magnet on a float rod work; or watch it and switch by hand.
- No DC pump: a small mains pump on an inverter wastes a lot of power but works with a battery and a big panel.

Water pumped from a stream or well isn't purified. Filter and boil or disinfect it before drinking.
